idiom_name: functools.singledispatch generic function: base implementation plus @register per element type
implementation_notes: Python's answer is a generic function: `@functools.singledispatch` wraps one callable whose decorated body is the default case and whose dispatch table is filled with `@fn.register(Type)` implementations, choosing by the first argument's type and falling back through the method resolution order to the base implementation (the docs: the original function 'is registered for the base object type, which means it is used if no better implementation is found'). Adding an element kind is then a registration anywhere in the program - no visitor class, no subclassing, nothing recompiled or edited - and `@functools.singledispatchmethod` does the same for methods, dispatching on the first non-self argument. The classic visitor-with-inheritance structure is still worth writing when an operation carries state and third parties must extend an existing implementation by inheriting it: singledispatch registration cannot be subclassed, so that case wants a visitor class hierarchy with isinstance-guarded dispatch and an overridable factory method.
pitfalls: Dispatch uses the runtime type of the first argument and walks the MRO: registering object (or a wide ABC) silently captures every type, and a later registration for a subclass changes results mid-run because the registry is global to the function.
singledispatchmethod must be the outermost decorator when combined with classmethod or staticmethod, and the dispatcher attribute is reachable on the class, not on instances.

Registrations are invisible to static checking: mypy cannot prove that every element type has a handler, so an unhandled kind shows up as the default path at runtime unless a test walks the hierarchy.
Registrations for the same type from two libraries overwrite each other silently; keep registration near the operation and document which types are claimed.
